scenario: AITA for being flakey? | So, I feel like an AH, so I need some help getting some perspective. Also, on mobile. I have a fairly close friend that I wish I could see more. We've gone through it. We worked at a minimum wage job together and graduated high school together. We're very different people now (she's married with a baby on the way, and I've been focused on my career), but when we get together it's great. Here's the AITA. When we graduated high school, I moved 4 hours away. Last week I moved 9 hours away from my home town and where she still lives. My parents never taught me how to drive, and it's never been necessary until recently to learn, so I always went back to hometown via a long (expensive) train ride. I now no longer see my parents, so going back would only be to see her. Now, dont get me wrong, I really do want to see my friend, but spending $300 for a weekend visit is a lot for me to swallow. I can afford it if I scrimped and saved every penny, but it would be very difficult. I'm also an introvert, so the idea of being a guest in someone's house for 3 days with no alone time makes me anxious. Because of this, I have cancelled more than a few times on plans (she has too, but less than I have), and I'm seriously considering not going to her baby shower because of the cost (I just moved and am sleeping on the floor because I cant afford a bed yet -.-) and the 9 hour trip. I feel like such a horrible friend. She has come to visit me (when I still lived only 4 hours away + they drove), and that just makes me feel worse. AITA for being a flaky friend?

First, the person has a close friend they've known since high school. They worked together at a minimum wage job and graduated together. Now, they're both in different life stages: the friend is married with a baby on the way, while the person is focused on their career. They moved 4 hours away after high school and recently moved another 5 hours further, making it a total of 9 hours from their hometown where their friend still lives. The person doesn't drive because their parents never taught them, and it wasn't necessary until recently. They used to take a long, expensive train ride to visit home, which cost $300 for a weekend. Now that they don't see their parents anymore, the only reason to go back is to visit their friend. They really want to see their friend but find the cost prohibitive. They also mention being an introvert, which makes the idea of spending three days at their friend's house without alone time anxiety-inducing. Because of these reasons, they've canceled plans more than a few times, and now they're considering not attending the friend's baby shower. They feel guilty about this, especially since their friend has made the effort to visit them when they were closer (4 hours away). The person is questioning if they're being a flaky friend. Now, to determine if they're AITA, I need to consider the context, their reasons, and the impact on the friendship. The person has valid reasons for not visiting: the high cost, being an introvert, and the recent move which has left them without a bed. They also express a genuine desire to see their friend but are constrained by practical issues. On the other hand, the friend has made efforts to visit, which might make the person feel worse. However, the friend's life situation is different—she's married with a baby, so visiting might be easier for her, especially since she can drive. The person's inability to drive adds another layer of difficulty. I think it's important to communicate these feelings and constraints to the friend. Explaining the reasons for canceling or not attending the baby shower could help the friend understand the situation better. It's not about being flaky but about facing real challenges. The person isn't ignoring the friendship; they're just dealing with obstacles that make maintaining the same level of contact difficult. In conclusion, while the person's actions might seem flaky on the surface, the underlying reasons are valid and understandable. They're not being a bad friend; they're just navigating their own circumstances. Open communication could help bridge any misunderstandings and strengthen the friendship.
